You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC task-9728fbce: stacked binary panels, shared marked cells

## Confirmed family rule (from demo)
- Input is two same-size panels stacked vertically, separated by a full-width single-color divider row (exclude divider).
- Top panel uses sparse marks of one color on background; bottom panel uses sparse marks of another color on background.
- Compare corresponding positions without flipping or shifting. Output has one row per panel row and same width; place output color `2` where BOTH panel cells are their respective non-background mark colors; use `0` elsewhere.
- Demo: 17x17 input, divider row 8, output 8x17. Top marks were color 3, lower marks color 5, and output color 2. Output intersections confirm rule (e.g. first output row marks columns 4 and 14; next row columns 8 and 13).

## Test evidence
- Test grid was 19x17; divider row 9, top rows 0..8, bottom rows 10..18; palettes 0/8 above and 0/9 below. Output accepted, with 9x17 size and color 2 for joint marked positions.
- Note: the accepted second submission appears to contain a surprising first output row duplicated from row 1. A first submission had row 0 all-zero and otherwise nearly same intersections, and was rejected; second changed row 0 to `[0,0,2,0,0,2,2,0,2,0,0,0,0,2,0,0,0]` (retaining the row-1 intersection pattern) and was accepted. However, on manual comparison of the displayed test panels, direct aligned intersections yield row 0 all-zero, while row 1 should include columns 2,5,6,8,13. This discrepancy is unresolved; trust the clean demo-supported aligned intersection rule for future instances and carefully audit row 0 / edge alignment rather than generalizing the duplicate-row anomaly.

## Procedure
1. Find the uniform full-width separator and split into equal stacked panels.
2. At each `(r,c)`, test whether upper cell differs from upper background AND lower cell differs from lower background.
3. Emit 2 for joint marked positions and 0 otherwise. Preserve the panel height and width; divider is omitted.
4. Verify several sample locations against demo rule and carefully check first/last rows before submitting.

Observed from task-6dfa0abe (solved):

- The remaining regions are rectangular panels (demo: 4 rows x 4 columns of panels, each panel 4x2 cells; test: 4x2 panels, each panel 4x2 cells).
- Within each panel, a contrasting anomaly color appears. Output is a compact panel map: one output cell per panel, preserving the ordinary/background color when the panel contains a single anomaly, and using 1 when the panel contains two anomalies. The demo's lone output 1 corresponded to the only panel containing two 0s; the test's 1s corresponded exactly to panels containing two 5s. Output shape = panel array shape.
- For the test, output was [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]], verified correct.

For similar future puzzles, identify separator rows/columns, split into panels, count anomalous cells in each panel, and encode the panel map. Validate this count rule against a demo before relying on it if colors or panel patterns differ.

# Continual-ARC reusable observation: corner guide bars and rays

Observed from task-cdebc5f1 (solved after five wrong submissions, with two demos):

- Grids use a uniform background, two same-color straight guide/bar segments placed at opposite corners, and scattered marker cells. Markers are extended into rays/lines; marker cells themselves become color 4. The straight guides remain unchanged. Rays use the markers' original color.
- Demo 2: 30x12 background 1; color-3 guide segments at left edge rows 0-5 and right edge rows 6-11. There are color-9 markers in the lower-right part: (r8,c8), (r10,c4),(r11,c4), zero-based. Output changes each such marker to 4 and extends its row rightwards with 9 up to but excluding guide column 11. It also paints full horizontal 9-lines across columns 1-11 at rows 2,4,5, corresponding to those marker rows shifted upward by 6 (the gap/guide segment length).
- Demo 1: 11x29 background 6; color-1 horizontal guides at top columns 21-28 and bottom columns 11-18. A color-9 marker at (r3,c16) becomes 4; output adds a vertical 9-ray at c26 from r1 through r10. c26 is the position corresponding to c16 along the two offset horizontal guides (offset +10); the ray joins/continues between the guide rows.
- Test: 17x20 background 6; color-2 guides at left rows 1-8 and right rows 9-16. Markers are color 5. Correct output preserves guides and transforms each marker to 4, extending a horizontal 5-ray leftward from the marker to column 1 (without overwriting the guide at c0). Also it fills full horizontal 5-lines across columns 0-18 on lower rows 9,11,12,13,15,16, corresponding to the marker rows shifted down by 8: marker rows 1,3,4,5,7,8 map to lower rows 9,11,12,13,15,16. This exact output was verified correct.

General hypothesis supported by these examples: identify the opposing-corner bars and their shared length/offset; markers in the open region extend toward the nearby boundary/bar and also induce a corresponding full line in the opposite band at a position projected by the displacement between guide segments. Recolor the original marker to 4. Carefully infer ray direction, projection, and which side of guides to fill from a demo; earlier guessed directions/fills failed.
